speaker: Moses Kagan
title: Repositioning 80 Apartment Buildings with Moses Kagan
question: In real estate syndication, why do value-add sponsors build an in-house property management arm even when it loses money at small unit counts?
guest: I always knew that to stabilize the platform—to be in a place where we didn't have to do a deal and weren't dependent on fees from any particular deal, so that if the market sucked we could just sit on our hands for a while—we were going to have to build a property management business. Property management fees are a recurring, smooth revenue stream that allows you to make payroll. In the beginning, we kept property management in-house even though we only had 10, 20, 50, or 100 units, and we would lose money on it. Every month we took precious deal fees from projects where we didn't even have ownership and used them to pay payroll for employees managing buildings we didn't own—so we were broke and subsidizing property management for rich people, which didn't feel great. Over time, as the portfolio grew through third-party referrals and buying more of our own deals, the property management business eventually became big enough to break even and turn profitable. It was a long slog, but it really paid off.

points.core: Relying solely on lumpy deal fees pressures sponsors into bad acquisitions for payroll.
points.note: Accept: transaction-dependent sponsors facing fixed overhead/payroll are forced to chase mediocre deals in poor markets just to keep lights on. Do not credit: generic statements about 'diversifying revenue' without explaining the perverse incentive to force deals.

points.core: Recurring property management revenue covers overhead so firms can pause buying during downturns.
points.note: Accept: smooth, predictable management fees stabilize the operating platform and allow sponsors to sit on their hands when market pricing is unattractive. Do not credit: claims that in-house management is only for better tenant service or lower maintenance costs without addressing platform stability.

points.core: Deal fees must subsidize unprofitable small management portfolios until unit count reaches breakeven.
points.note: Accept: early-stage in-house management loses money at low unit counts (e.g., 10–100 units) and requires cross-subsidy from transaction fees until scale turns it profitable. Do not credit: assuming in-house management is immediately profitable or ignoring the early-stage subsidy J-curve.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because the management company's own profit and loss is not the point; control over execution of the business plan is. A value-add deal makes its money by forcing net operating income upward through renovations, re-leasing at higher rents, expense cuts, and tighter collections. Every dollar of added NOI is capitalized into roughly $15–20 of property value at typical cap rates, and that value drives the sponsor's promote and track record. A 3% management fee is trivial by comparison.

Third-party managers are paid a percentage of collected revenue, so they have little incentive to push hard on renovation pace, rent bumps, or turnover speed. They also rotate staff, spread attention across many clients, and tend to give small portfolios their weaker teams. In-house management aligns incentives, gives the sponsor real-time data and direct control over staffing, leasing, and capex, and makes for a stronger pitch to investors and lenders.

Sponsors also treat early losses as an investment. The platform becomes profitable at scale (often cited around 1,500–3,000 units), captures management, construction-management, and ancillary fees that would otherwise leak out, and becomes a recurring-income business with its own enterprise value.

points.why: The response never connects dependence on deal fees for payroll to pressure to pursue mediocre acquisitions.
The response mentions recurring income without explaining how it covers overhead and lets sponsors pause acquisitions when pricing is unattractive.
The response acknowledges early losses and profitability at scale but never identifies deal fees as the subsidy that funds management until breakeven.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Value-add syndicators subsidize sub-scale, in-house property management because modest operating losses on the management P&L are dwarfed by the property-level equity and carried interest (promote) at stake. Third-party managers earn a percentage of gross collected revenue, creating misaligned incentives during turnarounds: they favor steady occupancy and minimal disruption, whereas value-add business plans require aggressive unit renovations, tenant turnover, and strict expense discipline that temporarily depress collections.

Bringing management in-house gives sponsors direct control over renovation turn times, leasing velocity, onsite staffing, and vendor pricing—the primary drivers of net operating income (NOI) and internal rate of return. Because commercial real estate is valued on a cap-rate multiple of NOI, even small operational improvements generate millions of dollars in exit value and sponsor promote, easily justifying an early management deficit. Vertical integration also provides proprietary, real-time rent and expense data for sharper acquisition underwriting, strengthens credibility with limited partners and lenders who prefer accountable operators, and establishes the operational infrastructure needed to reach standalone profitability once the portfolio scales.

points.why: The response does not explain how relying on deal fees to meet payroll can pressure sponsors into making bad acquisitions.
The response does not connect recurring management fees to covering overhead and giving sponsors the freedom to pause acquisitions.
The response acknowledges early management losses and eventual profitability at scale, but it does not identify deal fees as the source of the subsidy.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Value-add sponsors usually take on in-house management at a loss for control, not for the fee. The business plan depends on carrying out renovations, raising rents to market, cutting delinquency, and lowering expenses. A third-party manager juggling many owners' properties often doesn't share the sponsor's urgency or incentives. Running management themselves means sponsors can push the renovation schedule, train leasing staff on premium units, and see operating data in real time.

It's also a long-term bet. Management fees of roughly 3–4% of collected revenue don't cover a regional manager, systems, and staff at a few hundred units. As the portfolio grows past about 1,000–2,000 units, the overhead is spread across more units and the arm becomes profitable. It can then add ancillary income from construction management or insurance and pay steadier fees than the deal-by-deal promote.

There are softer benefits too. Lenders and LPs like a vertically integrated operator with a track record. Sponsors also keep their teams and know-how in-house and can underwrite new acquisitions more confidently, because they know what their own operations can actually do. One thing LPs should watch for: fees paid to the sponsor's own management company are a conflict of interest and should be scrutinized.

The response notes that management fees are steadier but never connects them to covering platform overhead so the sponsor can pause acquisitions.
The response explains early operating losses and eventual profitability at scale but omits the deal-fee subsidy that bridges the gap.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Value-add syndication sponsors often build in-house property management at a loss because the real payoff comes from asset-level equity creation, not management fee profit. Value-add business plans depend on intense daily execution—turning units quickly, controlling renovation and maintenance costs, pushing rents, and curbing delinquencies. Third-party managers are typically compensated on gross revenue across many competing clients, which incentivizes them to prioritize easy occupancy over maximizing net operating income. Because commercial properties are valued as a multiple of NOI, even modest operational slippage from a misaligned third-party manager can erase millions in equity at sale or refinance, dwarfing the management company's early operating deficit. Bringing management in-house gives sponsors direct control over hiring, pricing, vendor bidding, and real-time data, allowing faster pivots when market conditions shift. It also builds a scalable operational platform that reassures investors and eventually becomes self-sustaining once the portfolio crosses a critical unit count.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Value-add sponsors bring property management in-house because day-to-day operations determine whether the investment plan works. Direct control over leasing, collections, maintenance, and unit renovations lets the sponsor coordinate the work, see problems sooner, and adjust quickly. Better execution can raise net operating income and increase the property’s value at sale or refinance.

At low unit counts, management fees may fall short of covering supervisors, accounting, software, and other overhead. A sponsor may absorb that loss because the gains at the properties can outweigh it. As the portfolio grows, especially when properties are close together, the management arm can spread overhead across more units, share staff across properties, and retain fees that would otherwise go to a third-party manager.

The response does not connect recurring management fees to covering firm overhead and pausing acquisitions in unfavorable markets.
The response describes early losses and economies of scale but never identifies deal fees as the subsidy that sustains the management arm until breakeven.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Value-add sponsors bring property management in-house because their returns depend on how well the renovation and leasing plan works. An in-house team gives them direct control over renovation quality, how quickly units are ready to rent, and what rents they can achieve. It also gives them faster feedback. If upgraded apartments sit vacant, the sponsor can adjust pricing or change the scope of the next renovations.

At a small unit count, management fees may fall short of covering payroll and systems. The sponsor may still accept that loss if better execution raises the properties’ net operating income and, in turn, their value. As the portfolio grows, fees from more units can cover the same central overhead and eventually make the management arm profitable.
